paragraphs: A federal judge in Colorado has ordered the head of Immigration and Customs Enforcement's Denver field office, Nathan Rasper, to appear in court Monday amid concerns that immigration authorities violated judicial release orders by immediately re-arresting detainees, according to Fox News. The report says at least one re-arrest happened outside a detention facility.

U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney, a Biden appointee, issued a Nov. 5 order that followed an earlier ruling requiring the government to identify every Colorado case since Oct. 27 in which ICE re-detained someone within 12 hours of a court-ordered release. Federal officials identified 14 petitioners who were re-arrested, but their filing did not give precise timing. Sweeney directed them to provide exact dates and times and to identify any other people detained right after court-ordered releases.

The inquiry stems partly from Ramon Quintero Alvarez, who was released Oct. 27 and immediately taken back into custody, according to a government filing. On Nov. 3, government attorneys said they would not submit a brief defending the lawfulness of his continued detention. At a Nov. 4 hearing, where ICE Assistant Field Office Director Nichole Black testified under oath, Sweeney ordered Alvarez released and barred his re-detention unless the government shows at a bond hearing, by clear and convincing evidence, that he is a flight risk or a danger to the community.

The Department of Homeland Security says ICE complied with lawful court orders and that a release order does not permanently shield someone from enforcement. In a statement to Fox News Digital, DHS said ICE may seek re-arrest in a way that complies with the judicial decision, and it called the suggestion otherwise "nothing short of sabotage."
The government must file the requested information by 8 a.m. Monday, ahead of Rasper's appearance. Sweeney has not indicated whether she will pursue contempt proceedings.

Malaysia's king has warned that any challenge to his order granting jailed former Prime Minister Najib Razak house arrest could amount to defying his decree, according to Al Jazeera. The warning came a day after the attorney general blocked Najib's transfer from prison.

Najib, 73, was jailed for his role in the 1MDB sovereign wealth fund plunder. King Sultan Ibrahim granted him a conditional pardon in September, allowing him to serve the rest of his sentence at home if he paid a $12m fine. On Friday, the attorney general halted the move after the fine was paid, saying his office needed more clarification on the pardon.

In a statement Saturday, the king said there was nothing to clarify, calling the pardon "clear, evident and without any ambiguity" and saying it was not tied to other cases against Najib. He said that because all conditions were met, any argument questioning the order leads toward denying the king's order. Najib's lawyer, Farhan Shafee, said there was "no basis" to keep him in prison and that he must be moved immediately to his residence.

The Attorney General's Office said it was not challenging the king's authority and aimed to avoid conflict between orders in force and ensure no sentence was carried out unlawfully. It did not say whether Najib would be moved right away. Later, the prime minister's office said the attorney general was seeking an audience with the king to express an intent to comply, while insisting some legal questions could only be decided by a court.

The house arrest applies only to Najib's first conviction. He faces another 15 years after being found guilty last year in a separate 1MDB-linked case, with that sentence to begin after house arrest ends. He is appealing that verdict.

The Federal Aviation Administration has announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the United States are operational, according to The Guardian. The systems are online at Bartow Executive Airport in Florida and Kenai Municipal Airport in Alaska, with five more regional airports slated to receive the technology next.

The agency says the towers use advanced cameras and digital displays to give controllers a continuous 360-degree view of airport activity, including runways, taxiways and surrounding airspace. The FAA maintains the technology is not meant to replace human controllers but to give them greater visibility and more information. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement that controllers continue to keep aircraft safely separated and that the agency is giving them better technology to do so.

The rollout is part of a modernization effort aimed at replacing decades-old equipment, including copper telecommunications lines, floppy disks and paper strips used to track aircraft. Congress approved $12.5bn over five years in June 2025, and the Trump administration is seeking another $30bn. Bedford is scheduled to appear before the House transportation and infrastructure committee next week, where he is expected to face questions about the progress and challenges of the initiative.

The Guardian reports that concerns have been raised about the technology, noting wider unease about artificial intelligence. In September, the FAA introduced an AI software tool called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, or Smart. Staffing in control towers has also been under close scrutiny since a 2025 midair collision near Washington, DC, that killed 67 people and that authorities later deemed "100% preventable."

Candidates backed by the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC won many races in the midterms, but nearly two-thirds of the money it and linked groups spent went to candidates who lost, according to Al Jazeera, citing a tally by the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. The institute says about $55m of the $84m spent by AIPAC, its super PAC the United Democracy Project and related groups went to candidates who did not win.

By number of winners, the record is stronger. The day after the November 3 election, AIPAC said it had counted some 234 backed candidates from both parties as winners. Track AIPAC, which records the group's funding, says pro-Israel groups backed candidates in at least 32 of 35 Senate races. In 26 of them they spent over $100,000 on a candidate, and 21 of those candidates won.

Among the notable losses, the group and affiliated committees spent about $30m on Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan. According to the New York Times, AIPAC then put in another $9m for Republican Mike Rogers, who lost to Abdul El-Sayed, a critic of Israel. In Maine, AIPAC-linked groups gave more than $4.8m toward Senator Susan Collins, who lost to Troy Jackson. In California, Melissa Hernandez received over $6m in backing but lost to Aisha Wahab.

Trita Parsi of the Quincy Institute, which advocates less US foreign involvement, said candidates now find AIPAC's donations toxic. Rina Shah, a former GOP congressional aide, said taking AIPAC support is now a real topic even among Republicans. AIPAC said in October it would stop endorsing candidates and making direct contributions after this cycle, and said on X that its members intend to expand their political activism.

Australia's climate change minister, Chris Bowen, will lead negotiations among nearly 200 countries at the COP31 UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, starting Monday, according to The Guardian. Ahead of the talks, he dismissed concerns about whether Australia, a major fossil fuel producer, can help keep the world moving away from coal, gas and oil.

Australia is the world's second largest exporter of coal for power stations and the largest exporter of coal for steelmaking, and supplies about a fifth of global liquefied natural gas. The government expects the three fuels to earn $141bn (US$98bn) this financial year. Turkey and Australia compromised after both sought to host: Turkey is president of the conference and Australia president of the negotiations.

Bowen named three priorities: limiting overshoot past the 1.5C Paris goal, helping poorer countries access finance, and a new 2035 goal, backed by Turkey and Australia, for 35% of final energy use worldwide to come from electricity. He said all countries are dealing with the transition and that Australia's domestic move away from coal power has been recognized internationally.

Detailed plans to transition away from fossil fuels are not on the official agenda. Climate Analytics chief executive Bill Hare said Australia could continue the roadmap process and that Bowen "needs to be brave." Economist Frank Jotzo said he doubted all countries would agree, and expected the Australian presidency to "play this very safe."

More than 500 mostly Australian scientists and academics wrote to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese asking him to end coal and gas approvals, saying that approving new projects while championing climate finance "invites the charge of hypocrisy." Domestically, the opposition Coalition has pledged to scrap the 2050 net zero target. The Albanese government's response to the letter was not reported.

Richard Lloyd, a founding member and guitarist of the influential punk band Television, has died at 75, according to The Guardian. His family said he died Saturday morning at his home in Chattanooga, Tennessee. In a statement to Rolling Stone, they said his wife, Sheila, and his dog, Willie Mays, were with him at the end.

The family said the cause was cholangiocarcinoma, a form of bile duct cancer, diagnosed in March 2026. A crowdfunding campaign had disclosed that Lloyd developed tumors in his liver and that one could not be surgically removed.

Television formed in 1973 and played a significant role in the emerging punk rock movement centered on CBGB, the former venue on the Bowery in New York City. The band was among the earliest punk acts to play there, at a club that had previously focused mainly on country and bluegrass. In a 2007 interview, Lloyd reflected on his part in the club's history, calling CBGB the most famous rock 'n' roll club ever and saying he was the "invisible force behind it."

Television recorded just two studio albums during its peak in the late 1970s. The first, Marquee Moon, released in 1977, has since been widely recognized as a landmark recording. Rolling Stone ranked it No 107 on its 2023 list of the 500 greatest albums of all time, and it is still considered one of the most influential guitar-driven albums in rock history.
The Guardian's 2005 review of a Lloyd performance said his guitar was louder in a lopsided mix and that he delivered crisp, crunchy chords, dextrous fills and torrential Van Halen-style solos.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog has chosen Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, to try to form the next government, passing over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Al Jazeera reported. Herzog told Eisenkot on Saturday evening, and the president's spokesperson said the mandate will be formally handed over at a ceremony on Sunday.

Herzog held consultations this week after neither side won a majority in the October 27 election. According to Al Jazeera, 67 lawmakers, including from Arab-led parties, endorsed Eisenkot, while 46 backed Netanyahu. Eisenkot's four-party alliance won 48 seats and Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc won 53. Arab-led parties won a record 19.

Eisenkot has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension, to assemble at least 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats. He has ruled out a government with Arab-led parties. Al Jazeera said that winning the two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61. He could also govern with fewer seats if he wins a confidence vote.

Ahmad Tibi of the Joint List said he expects a minority government with external support from Arab parties, and that his priority is bringing down the government of Netanyahu, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich. Hours before the decision, Netanyahu said in a video that a government dependent on Islamists would dismantle Israel from within. Tibi rejected Netanyahu's description of Arab-led parties as supporters of terrorism.

If Eisenkot fails, Herzog will nominate another candidate. If that candidate also fails, a parliamentary majority can back a third, who would get a final 14 days. If no government forms, a new election would be called within 90 days, with Netanyahu staying on as caretaker prime minister.

President Donald Trump has publicly asked UFC chief Dana White to become White House press secretary, according to the BBC. In a Truth Social post on Saturday, Trump wrote that White "will be a Press Secretary like none other" and urged: "Dana, please take the job!" The BBC said it is unclear whether the offer is genuine, and it had asked the White House, the UFC and its parent company TKO Group Holdings for comment.

The job has been vacant since mid-October, when Katie Zacharia left after just a few days. Trump's post came after Republicans lost their congressional majorities in the midterm elections. He also asked White to bring several UFC fighters with him, saying they were needed to defend against the "Lunatic Left".

After the post, White shared an Instagram photo of himself behind the lectern in the White House briefing room, captioned "On to the next chapter." The BBC said it was unclear whether that was tongue-in-cheek. White was at a boxing event in London on Saturday, and the BBC was trying to reach him.

White is a longtime Trump ally. The BBC noted that he has spoken at Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024, and that the UFC held a cage match on the White House lawn this summer. It also described him as combative with journalists at times.
The BBC said it is far from clear he would have time for the role. He leads the UFC and Power Slap, has just launched Zuffa Boxing, and became a Meta board member last year.

President Donald Trump said in a Saturday Truth Social post that he has ordered the Justice Department to investigate Democrats he accused of threatening people with impeachment and other punishment. He called it "extortion at the highest level" and a "criminal act". Al Jazeera noted that he offered no evidence for the claim.

The post followed Democratic wins in Tuesday's midterms. Fox News reported Democrats retook the House and Senate. Fox said Reps. Hank Johnson and Deborah Ross have publicly said they would support impeaching Attorney General Todd Blanche, with Ross saying Democrats should start with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Trump said no impeachable acts had been committed. Fox also reported that Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican, will likely reintroduce impeachment articles against Hegseth on Monday.

Trump named one Democrat, Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, accusing her of saying she would go after young people who hold Republican values. Fox said he appeared to be referring to an October 13 speech in which she spoke of pursuing "signature cases" against people who enabled Trump, and of sending a "deterrence message" to young people weighing jobs in his administration. Al Jazeera said he gave no evidence she threatened people over their views. The reports did not include a response from Slotkin.

Trump also said Democrats were threatening Republican donors with imprisonment, without naming any. Fox cited Reuters as reporting that Democrats plan to investigate some major donors and corporations.
When Democrats take control in January, Al Jazeera said, they can demand documents, summon officials to testify and hold hearings.

Protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday for a fourth consecutive weekend. Al Jazeera, citing the Interior Ministry, reported about 146,000 people rallied nationwide, including 46,000 in Paris. Unions gave higher figures: 250,000 nationwide and 75,000 in the capital.

Turnout was lower than in previous weeks, but clashes still broke out in Paris. Footage posted by the CLPRESS agency showed police charging protesters and using tear gas, and an officer hitting a protester with a baton. Police told AFP that 200 people attacked officers who were arresting a man accused of setting fire to a rubbish bin. In Lyon, police fired tear gas at several hundred people blocking a road at an unauthorised gathering.
About 70,000 security personnel were deployed. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said authorities would be "ready and waiting" for anyone rioting or looting.

The movement began in September over poor conditions and scarce resources at French high schools, then widened to cover worsening living standards. Students still lead it, but people of all ages take part. Al Jazeera's Natacha Butler said unions, weakened in recent years, feel a sense of momentum and want to press the government for higher salaries. A rally organised by trade unions days earlier drew an estimated 575,000 people.

The protests come ahead of an April presidential election. Polls put Marine Le Pen of the National Rally first, followed by Jean-Luc Melenchon of France Unbowed, who unveiled his programme to some 17,000 supporters on Saturday and promised to do the opposite of President Emmanuel Macron.

Nine people are now known dead after a shooting in Kraków's Main Market Square on Saturday, according to the Guardian and the BBC. Polish authorities said six people were killed and 16 wounded in the square. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said late Saturday that two women and a man were also found dead at the suspect's home, most likely family members.

The attack began shortly before 3 p.m. Police said a man drove into the square and fired at random people from his car. A passing tram was also shot at, though the BBC said no passengers were hurt. Officials said armed officers shot the attacker within three minutes. He is alive and under arrest.

Four women and two men died in the square, including a British citizen. Three of the victims are Polish, and two had not been identified. Among the wounded are five foreigners and two police officers; one officer was shot three times and is in very critical condition.

Police described the suspect as a 25-year-old Polish citizen who is not a soldier. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said he was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held "very radical" and "ultra-nationalistic" views. Polish media reported he held a firearms permit. Police found weapons and ammunition in his car, which was checked for explosives, and his home is being searched with counter-terrorism police.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz called it an act of terror, and Tusk used similar language. National mourning will be observed on Sunday and Monday, and the BBC said Kraków's mourning lasts until Wednesday.

Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago Pena with breach of trust and administration for personal gain, according to the BBC and Al Jazeera, which cited Reuters. Pena denies wrongdoing. The charges come a day after senators impeached him over the collapse of Ueno Bank.

Al Jazeera reported that Pena spent Saturday morning at the attorney general's office for questioning and had been under house arrest since Friday. Prosecutors are seeking pretrial detention for him and for Carlos Carvallo, the central bank head he appointed in 2023, who was also charged. Al Jazeera said Pena held a stake in Ueno's parent company until March 2025.

The allegations include conflicts of interest, shielding the bank from regulatory scrutiny, steering public funds to it, and letting the state pension fund deposit $355 million there, above legal limits. Pena argued the bank's problems were a regulatory matter. His lawyer, Ricardo Preda, called the accusation reckless and opportunistic.

Regulators took control of Ueno on Tuesday over solvency concerns, leaving an estimated three million people unable to reach their savings. Paraguay's central bank said 1.2 million customers had received partial or full reimbursement of insured deposits. Protests have continued, some with clashes with police.

Pena offered to resign, but senators proceeded with impeachment, which the BBC said removes the immunity usually given to ex-presidents. The vote was 44 of 45 senators. Pedro Alliana, now interim president until 2028, promised that affected people will be fully compensated. Al Jazeera said he is himself under investigation over the collapse, and some protesters are frustrated by his appointment.

Houthi-run media said air strikes on a village in Sanaa province on Saturday killed at least 25 people, with Houthi-run Saba news agency later citing a toll of 27 and about 30 wounded. Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesman for the Sanaa-based health ministry, said most casualties were women and children. The BBC and Al Jazeera both said they could not independently verify the reports.

The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia and its coalition. The BBC said there had been no comment from the coalition, and Al Jazeera said neither Saudi Arabia nor the Yemeni government had commented on these strikes. Houthi leader Mahdi al-Mashat vowed to take revenge. Hours earlier, coalition spokesman Colonel Turki al-Malki said a Houthi ballistic missile was shot down over the Riyadh region.

The strikes follow a Friday attack on a market in Taiz province that reportedly killed 30 people. The Houthis blamed Saudi strikes, while government forces said the Houthis fired a missile. Al Jazeera's Yousef Mawry said the Houthis put the civilian toll over two days at 55, while government officials hold the Houthis responsible for most casualties.

The BBC said the war, dormant for years, reignited because of the Iran war, and the United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed. On Saturday, government forces said they repelled Houthi assaults in Marib and were pushing into al-Jawf, and claimed to have neutralised about 130 Houthi fighters. Al Jazeera could not verify this. The Houthis said they launched six attacks on Saudi targets.

Dave Wehner, Meta's chief strategy officer, is leaving the company to become chief financial officer of Fireworks, an AI startup, CNBC reported. Wehner announced the move on X on Friday. Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao said he will be tasked with scaling the company's finances and operations.

Fireworks, founded in 2022 by former Meta and Google employees, runs an AI inference and model-training platform that lets developers customize and run open models. It was valued at $17.5 billion in a Series D round in July led by Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV, and it is also backed by Nvidia and Sequoia Capital. CNBC said Business Insider reported the company is in early talks to raise again at a possible $30 billion to $40 billion valuation.

Wehner joined Meta, then called Facebook, in 2012 and served as chief financial officer from 2014 to 2022. Meta COO Javier Olivan said Wehner guided the company through 14 years of growth and complexity. Wehner wrote that he has become "increasingly bullish" on Fireworks, citing its technical talent and practical focus on customers. Qiao said he wanted to return to a smaller company where he could build toward a big impact again.

CNBC noted that Fireworks is far smaller than Meta, which had a market capitalization of about $1.56 trillion at Friday's close. In October, Fireworks disclosed a security incident in which an unauthorized third party accessed environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. The company said it had not detected unauthorized access to customer models, datasets, personal information or inference traffic.

NASA has opened applications for its next class of astronauts. According to the agency, those selected will join as the United States returns to the Moon, builds what NASA calls the Moon Base, and lays groundwork for the first crewed Mars missions. U.S. citizens have until 11:59 p.m. EST on Thursday, Dec. 3, to apply. NASA expects to make its final selection in late 2027.

Applicants need U.S. citizenship and a master's degree in a STEM field, though the requirement can also be met through two years of doctoral work, a medical degree, or a qualifying test pilot school program completed by July 2027. Candidates need at least three years of related professional experience. Pilots can meet it through set flight hours, such as 750 hours as pilot in command of high-performance jets. Medical residency may count if completed by July 2027. Candidates must also pass NASA's long-duration astronaut flight physical and show strong leadership, teamwork and communication skills.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said the people selected could walk on the Moon and help pioneer the systems that will carry crews to Mars. Chief astronaut Scott Tingle called it a chance to join a legacy of explorers.

The agency last opened applications in 2024. From more than 8,000 applications, 10 candidates were selected in 2025 and are completing nearly two years of training. NASA said it has selected 370 people for astronaut candidate training since the 1960s and has 32 active astronauts. New astronauts will study spacewalking, lunar geology and the operation of high-performance aircraft, among other subjects.
